paragraphs.text: Combined cycle power plants have emerged as a promising economic solution for escalating global energy demand. So, the researchers always have a non-end competition for more improvements of cycle design of the fossil fuel power plants in terms of capacity, and efficiency, and pointing to most components requires a potential optimization as well. This study presents and analyzes the performance of a novel modification on a combined cycle power plant that is mainly designed to reduce the effect of intercooling on CCPP efficiency degradation. As well as handing over the detailed chemical and physical combustion process exergy analysis using energy and exergy approaches under on-design and off-design operating conditions. The results yielded an increase in the efficiency of SCC5-8000H CCPP by 0.26% and marginal output power enhancement by 14.5 MW. While the exergy destruction of the whole power plant decreased by 41.23 MW.

Appropriate energy sources management especially electricity would be a pillar and fulcrum for nations’ economic development, civilization, globalization, and international relations improvement that all stakeholders intend to have in the most profitable and economical form as showed by (Gellings, 2020; Yu et al., 2019). The last uprising in energy prices worldwide due to geopolitically wars motivated the forefront attention of all nations to get energy economically and cleaner by depending on renewable energy sources. Despite the high initial cost, the low availability of RES made the CCPP unparalleled in mastering the produced power and most preferable as (Neha and Rambeer, 2021) claimed. The CCPPs significantly affect the global energy demand due to their dominance in the power generation sector. This dominance is because of their high efficiency, which can exceed 60%, and their high reliability as well. Also, the CCPPs are characterized by high availability due to fuel variety dependence as well as operational flexibility, as they can quickly adjust to changes in electricity demand, providing the necessary flexibility to complement intermittent renewable energy sources like wind and solar which will result in grid stability. Also, they function as base load or peak load power sources. Furthermore, many advanced CCPPs may be powered by natural gas, and others can run on clean hydrogen fuel. This is not to announce that CCPPs or RES plants will be the exclusive market leaders. However, both of them are involved in electricity generation for a purpose. The RES plants are designed to cut emissions and achieve zero carbon emissions. While the CCPPs operate, they will adjust their output to balance fluctuations caused by various renewable energy sources. So, CCPPs allowed non-end competition to design the best flexible and performance-enhancing cycle regarding energy, exergy, economic, and environmental concerns.

Studies proposed different retrofitting cycles with performance investigation for optimization purposes; (Briesch et al., 1995) discussed the technologies and components under development. As well as limitations of parametric optimization and cycle retrofitting including TIT, CPR, intercooling, recuperation, reheat, and thermochemical recuperation to exceed CCPP efficiency of 60%. (Dellenback, 2002) proposed an alternative recuperated gas turbine cycle and claimed that the proposed cycle would exhibit the highest efficiency compared to the conventional recuperated cycle. (Cai and Jiang, 2006) analyzed the alternative recuperated cycle proposed by (Dellenback, 2002) and showed off the reasonability of this analysis results in the ideal case of the cycle. However, with irreversibility consideration, the proposed alternative recuperated cycle will not be the highest efficiency. (Gogoi, 2014) performed a comparative performance study among conventional and recuperated CCPP. This study showed that CCPP with both air and fuel recuperators is the most efficient cycle. (Mostafa, Eldrainy and EL-Kassaby, 2018) investigated the performance of simple and recuperated gas turbine cycles and proved that employing inlet fogging with overspray systems can reduce compressor power consumption by 12% at high ambient temperatures. (Sanjay and Prasad, 2013) investigated air film cooling and novel closed-loop steam bucket cooling systems on IC-GT- 3P CCPP performance using energy and exergy analysis. The study showed that air film cooling technology demonstrates higher efficiency. (Kayadelen, Ust and Bashan, 2021) performed an optimization study of simple, reheat, steam-injected, and reheated steam-injected gas turbine cycles based on CPR variation at different reheat pressure ratios and steam injection rates. (Khan, 2021b) investigated the proposal of splitting combustion gases between gas turbine and HRSG at different pressure and air-fuel ratios.

The peak efficiency and power were found at maximum pressure ratio and minimum air-fuel ratio with no combustible gases bypassing the gas turbine expansion section. Also, many studies have presented the effect of SF systems on cycle performance; (Abdollahian and Ameri, 2021; Mokhtari, Esmaieli and Hajabdollahi, 2016) investigated the SF effect on CCPP’s performance using energy and exergy approaches under different operating modes, condenser pressure, CPR, and fuel LHV variation. The studies showed that SF increases the generated power with a slight decrease in thermal efficiency. Many studies have been conducted to optimize energy recovery management through repowering steam power plants and extending ORC as a bottoming cycle; (Ahmed and Oudah, 2018) proposed repowering of the AL-Mussaib steam power plant and investigated its performance under different operating conditions. The study showed that ambient temperature is the most effective parameter for performance. While, (Bǎlǎnescu and Homutescu, 2019; Hemadri and Subbarao, 2021) proposed and analyzed the performance of ORC as a bottoming cycle of CCPP and RH-ORC as a bottoming cycle for gas turbines, respectively. Other different studies investigated the performance of already existing combined cycles under different operating modes as; (Altarawneh et al., 2022; Al-Qudaha et al., 2020) performed energy and exergy investigation on 400 MW KOSPO CCPP and Al-Qatrana Power Plant (AQPP), respectively under full load and 75% load using natural gas and diesel fuel oil. These studies showed that full-load operation using natural gas is the best choice for the sake of efficiency and output power. (Egware and Obanor, 2022) investigated the energy performance of the SGT5-2000E gas turbine under CPR, TIT, and ambient temperature variation.

The results emphasized that power and efficiency have indirect relation against ambient temperature increment and can be enhanced by CPR and TIT increment. (Mohd Saif and Tariq, 2017) showed that ambient temperature and CPR are the most affecting parameters on simple gas turbine cycle performance. (Albishti and Dabashi, 2019) verified the design point and evaluated the off-design performance of simple and intercooled aero-derivative gas turbine cycles over ambient temperature, elevation, and power variation. The study unveiled that the intercooled cycle performance was less affected by ambient temperature variation. (El-Badri et al., 2022) investigated the performance of different gas turbines in open and combined cycles at the location of the North Benghazi power plant under ambient temperature and humidity variation. (Jamnani et al., 2021) investigated the performance of different gas turbine configurations in 3PR CCPP and showed that the combustion chamber has the highest exergy destruction while the air compressor has the lowest irreversibility destruction. (Almutairi and Alenezi, 2019) analyzed the performance of Al Sabiya CCPP with various topping gas cycle engines and showed that the best choice for the highest power, efficiency, and lowest exergy destruction was the gas turbine with the highest CPR. Many studies have investigated the performance of power plants based on energy and exergy approaches as; (Moussa, Hassan and El-Fouly, 2021; Chen et al., 2022) performed 2E performance analyses on 4800 MW CCPP located in Beni-Suef, Egypt, and Banshan power plant located in Hangzhou, China under ambient temperature and humidity variation. (Babaei Jamnani and Kardgar, 2020) investigated a 396 MW CCPP located in the Malay Peninsula based on energy and exergy approaches with reference temperature, pressure ratios, condenser and reheat pressure variations.

(Ibrahim et al., 2017) analyzed the performance of the MARAFEQ Power plant in Saudi Arabia. On the other hand, (Aliyu et al., 2020) analyzed the performance of 1.24 GW CCPP located in the eastern province of Saudi Arabia based on energy and exergy analyses under ambient temperature variation. Also, (Şen et al., 2018) investigated the performance of a 240 MW CCPP located in Aliağa, İzmir, Turkey using energy and exergy analyses under ambient temperature variation. while (Abuelnuor et al., 2024) analyzed a steam cycle power plant located in Khartoum, Sudan based on energy and exergy approaches. All these studies concluded that the combustion chamber is the major source of potential destruction in the whole cycle. Other studies emphasized the importance of optimizing the condenser pressure for overall cycle performance enhancement as (Alus, Elrawemi and Eldabee, 2017; Laskowski et al., 2021; Pattanayak, Padhi and Kodamasingh, 2019) presented a universally applicable model for condenser simulation based on standards for steam surface condensers (Heat Exchanger Institute, 2012). Many studies regarded the future of CCPP in the era of developing RES power plants. (Alberto Boretti, 2025) pointed toward fuels that can be used in gas turbine engines and CCPP such as free-carbon ammonia and the promising transitional green hydrogen fuel and their roles in the future of CCPP operation toward net zero, as they can accommodate a fuel mixture with green hydrogen to pure hydrogen only as the main fuel used.

According to the literature review, previous studies either conducted on performance investigations of thermal power plants or gave different proposals for performance optimization. These studies have confirmed that the CCPP's performance deteriorates during operation beyond its stipulated design conditions, especially in hot climates, since ambient temperature increase is the reason behind the reduced CCPP performance, including output power and thermal energy efficiency, and therefore significant waste energy and emissions released into the environment. Also, the previous studies conducted on performance investigation did not address all of the parameters that influence energy and exergy analysis accuracy. Additionally, the analysis was performed regardless of the chemical compositions of air, fuel, and product combustion gases, and it was assumed that natural gas is pure Methane, which is not true. However, all studies showed that the combustion chamber is the major source of potential destruction. Therefore, the CCPP is in a conundrum due to the renewable energy resources trend, which makes it challenging for all researchers to develop a retrofitted cycle that improves the performance under ambient temperature variation.

One of the most commonly known retrofitting is the intercooled gas turbine combined cycle which plays a vital role in boosting output power and decreasing the significant effect of ambient temperature variation on the overall performance. However, in many cases, the resultant thermal efficiency may slightly decrease since the compressed air entering the combustion chamber at a relatively lower temperature will consume a higher amount of fuel to reach TIT. Therefore, the heat addition increases and there is higher exergy destruction in the combustion chamber. Also, the intercooler operating pressure and pressure loss will affect the exhaust gas temperature and flow rate passing through the HRSG. So, this study's main objectives are to present and investigate the proposed modification to the conventional intercooled gas turbine combined cycle to overcome the efficiency drawback, maximize the heat recovery capability that will reflect on decreasing the exergy destruction on the overall CCPP, and hand over guidelines for exergy analysis of hydrocarbon and natural gas combustion with-respect- to its composition that is supplied to El-Burullus CCPP for ultimate analysis accuracy. The results are validated against one of the largest and most efficient SCC5-8000H CCPP worldwide located in Kafr El-Shaikh province, Burullus, Egypt with technical specifications published by Siemens [37-41].

El-Burullus CCPP is located in Kafr el-Shaikh province and is considered the largest and the most efficient CCPP in Egypt and even in the world. Similar to the Beni-Suef CCPP that was described by (Moussa, Hassan and El-Fouly, 2021). This plant consists of four modules each of 2 x 2 x 1 configuration with 4800 MW total capacity and thermal efficiency exceeds 60% at ISO operating conditions. Each module consists of two SGT5-8000H gas turbines, two triple-pressure reheat HRSGs, one set of steam turbines operating at three different pressures, and three generators. The gas turbine consists of three main components: compressor, combustion chamber, and turbine section. These two gas turbine engines are fired with preheated natural gas up to 215℃ during combined cycle operation and the flue gas is fed through a bypass stack with a diverter damper to both unfired vertical three-pressure reheat HRSG for steam generation at three different pressure levels that are directed toward the steam turbines. The expanded steam is condensed in a steam surface condenser that is aligned to the LP turbine and utilizes recirculating cooling water from the cooling tower.

According to the last Egyptian energy report 2022/2023 submitted by EEHC (Egyptian Electricity Holding Company, 2023), Egypt has a surplus electricity capacity as this plant operates at a 61.33% loading factor only. Thus, the main objective of this study is to enhance efficiency. One of the most popular retrofits is conventional intercooling which utilizes two compressors and an intercooler to lower the air temperature before the second compression stage using an open cooling water source or air that is usually discarded. So, the main objective of conventional intercooling retrofitting is boosting the net output power. However, efficiency isn’t necessarily enhanced.

According to conventional intercooling investigation that is applied on El-Burullus CCPP, the power output is noticeably enhanced as much as the ambient air temperature and compressed air temperature are lowered before entering the high-pressure compressor. However, the resultant compressed air temperature will be lower than the conventional cycle which results in higher exergy destruction, higher fuel consumption, and therefore lower thermal energy efficiency. So, the current study examines several alternative intercooling retrofitting proposals with the optimum selection of intercooler pressure and different other parameters for optimization purposes.

Utilizing a partial amount of the bottoming cycle’s economizing water at three different pressures for the gas turbine’s intercooler, either by itself solely or in combination with reheating or regeneration retrofitting, is the primary foundation of these alternative intercooling retrofitting concepts. Additionally, there are other suggestions based on alternative intercooling accompanied by bypassing the flue gases between two HRSGs and, lastly, the state-of-the-art alternative intercooling accompanied by a steam injection system. All these proposals are put forth to save a portion of flue gas’ heat energy to be subsequently utilized.

The study yielded that the optimum cycle proposal is based on utilizing the low-pressure economizing water as a coolant for the intercooler and accompanied by a steam injection system for the sake of power and efficiency degrading enhancement that is accompanied by conventional intercooling retrofitting. The proposed cycle layout is depicted in Figure 1, which illustrates that the air enters the LP compressor after passing through a series of filters and is subsequently cooled before the HP compressor using varying amounts of the low-pressure economizing water for lower compression power consumption, higher work ratio, water preheating, and trading off between higher cycle power capacity or efficiency since high amount of coolant leads to increase gas turbine output power and decrease the thermal efficiency. The air and preheated natural gas are mixed and burned to produce high-pressure and temperature flue gases that expand through gas turbines and are directed to HRSG through a bypass stack with a diverter damper for steam generation at three different pressure levels. The preheated economizing water outlet from the intercooler is mixed with the remaining amount of the water before entering the LP economizer which contributes to saving a portion of flue gas heat energy.

This heat energy is subsequently exploited through an additional small-capacity evaporator and economizer that are placed at the end of HRSG at the stack section which is designed to produce saturated steam which will be injected into the LP steam turbine at an appropriate pressure. The steam-injected system is an additional mechanism that primarily utilizes the energy present in flue gases after they pass through the LP economizer, before being released into the environment. This process can be achieved by pumping varying quantities of water, which becomes saturated and is then injected into the steam turbine, helping to maintain the flue gas temperatures released into the atmosphere at a lower level, approximately 80 degrees Celsius. This innovation is set to transform the design of Combined Cycle Power Plants (CCPP) by enhancing the operational flexibility of gas turbines, allowing for a balance between output and efficiency, as well as improving heat recovery capabilities since the temperature of the flue gases exiting the stack is regulated by the volume of water used in the supplemental steam injection system.
Figure 1. Proposed layout of an intercooled gas turbine three-pressure reheat combined cycle with a saturated steam injection system.

The analysis of the SGT5-8000H Gas Turbine and SCC5-8000H CCPP was performed based on energy and exergy approaches under on-design and off-design operating conditions at the plant location with the help of a MATLAB R2017a that was developed specifically for this purpose concerning the following assumptions: 1. All components associated with the cycle are considered as an open system with steady-state flow. 2. Working fluids (Air and flue gases) are considered ideal gases with neglected cooling airflow rates. 3. Extracted cooling compressed air mass flow rate for turbine blades cooling is neglected. 4. Constant turbine inlet temperature = 1647.15 K. 5. Intercooler and combustion chamber pressure drop = 1%. 6. Combustion process efficiency = 99%. 7. Potential and kinetic energies will be neglected for simplifications. 8. Fuel preheating exergy destruction is relatively small and can be neglected. All processes are adiabatic.

The energy analysis approach is based on the first law of thermodynamics. It is used in all thermal systems to show off its capability and efficiency regardless of the location and quantity of irreversibilities causing that efficiency [43].

The specific heat at a constant pressure of air is a function of temperature [44] and can be obtained from equation (1) and equation (2) for air temperature ranges from 250 K to 599 K and 600 K to 1500 K respectively. C_p_air = {1.023204 − [(1.76021 x 10^−4) T] + [(4.0205 x 10^−7) T^2] − [(4.87272 x 10^−11) T^3]} (1) (specific heat of air at constant pressure as a cubic function of air temperature T, for 250 K to 599 K) C_p_air = {0.874334 − [(3.22814 x 10^−4) T] + [(3.58694 x 10^−8) T^2] − [(1.99196 x 10^−11) T^3]} (2) (specific heat of air at constant pressure as a cubic function of air temperature T, for 600 K to 1500 K) The actual pressurized air temperature outlet from the compressor and consumption power can be obtained from the following equation (3) and equation (4) T_out,comp = T_in,comp [(P_r_comp)^((γ_air−1)/γ_air) − 1 + η_comp,is] / η_comp,is (3) (actual compressed air outlet temperature from inlet temperature, compressor pressure ratio, specific heat ratio and isentropic efficiency) Ẇ_compressor = ṁ_air C_p_air T_in [(P_r_comp)^((γ_air−1)/γ_air) − 1] / (η_Comp,is η_mech) (4) (compressor consumption power)

paragraphs.text: In the case of an intercooled cycle, the intercooler’s effectiveness and cooled compressed air outlet temperature can be obtained from the following equations (5, 6); ε_I.C = [ṁ_air C_P_air (T_in − T_out)] / [C_min (T_in − T_water_in)] (5) (intercooler effectiveness = actual heat removed from the air / maximum possible heat transfer based on C_min and the inlet temperature difference) T_air,out = T_air,in − {[ε_I.C C_min (T_in − T_water_in)] / (ṁ_air C_P_air)} (6) (cooled compressed air outlet temperature from the intercooler effectiveness)

The mass and heat balance of the combustion chamber can be evaluated according to equation (7); Q̇_C.C = [(ṁ_gas C_p_gas TIT) − (ṁ_air C_p_air T_c.c,in)] / η_C.C (7) (combustion chamber heat addition rate = enthalpy rise from compressed air to gas at TIT, divided by combustion chamber efficiency) From the mass and heat balance of the combustion chamber, the fuel-to-air ratio (F/A) concerning the physical properties of fuel at constant TIT can be obtained from the following equation (8); F/A = [((C_p_gas TIT) − (C_P_air T_c.c,in)) / ((η_combustion LHV) − (C_p_gas TIT) + (C_p_fuel T_fuel))] (8) (fuel-to-air ratio from the combustion chamber heat balance at constant TIT)

The turbine pressure ratio depends on pressure drop in the combustion chamber, intercooler, and back pressure on the turbine. This ratio can be obtained as follows from the following equation (9). P_r_Turbine = P_(s.c) P_r_comp [1−(ΔP_I.C%/100)] [1−(ΔP_C.C%/100)] / P_exit GT (9) (turbine pressure ratio from compressor pressure ratio reduced by intercooler and combustion chamber pressure drops, divided by turbine exit back pressure) The produced power from the gas turbine stages can be obtained from the following equation (10); Ẇ_Turbine = ṁ_gas C_p_gas TIT η_mech η_Turb,is [(P_r_Turbine)^((γ_g−1)/γ_g) − 1] / (P_r_Turbine)^((γ_g−1)/γ_g) (10) (power produced by the gas turbine stages) The overall energy performance indicators for the gas turbine cycle include thermal energy efficiency, net output power, and specific fuel consumption that can be obtained from the following equations (11-13) respectively. η_en = (Ẇ_Turbine − Ẇ_compressor) / Q̇_C.C (11) (gas turbine cycle thermal energy efficiency), Ẇ_net = Ẇ_Turbine – Ẇ_compressor (12) (net output power), SFC = 3600 ṁ_fuel / Ẇ_net (13) (specific fuel consumption)

The pressurized water is heated to produce superheated steam at three different pressures in the HRSG that is arranged into four sections: reheater section, high-pressure section, intermediate-pressure section, and low-pressure section respectively. As terminal temperature difference (TTD), pinch points, and approach points for the three pressures are known, the flue gas temperature after passing the reheater, steam generation rate at the high-pressure section, and the gas temperature at the end of the high-pressure section can be obtained from equation (14 – 16); T_gas,in_hp−sh = T_hp−st + 273.15 + TTD = T_gas,out_GT − ΔT_across−R.H (14) (flue gas temperature after the reheater = HP steam temperature + 273.15 + terminal temperature difference = GT exhaust gas temperature − temperature drop across the reheater) ṁ_st_h = {[ṁ_gas C_p_gas (T_gas,in_hp−sh − T_gas,out_hp−evap) (1 − heat loss%)] − [blow down% (h_sat,in_hp−evap − h2h)]} / (h_hp−sh−outlet − h_hp−evap−inlet) (15) (high-pressure steam generation rate from the gas-side heat balance over the HP superheater and evaporator, less blowdown) T_gas,out_hp−eco = T_gas,out_hp−evap − [ṁ_st_h (h_hp−evap−inlet − h_hp−eco−inlet) / (ṁ_gas C_p_gas)] (16) (gas temperature at the end of the high-pressure section, after the HP economizer)

The intermediate and low-pressure steam generation rates can be obtained as follows in equations (17, 18) respectively: ṁ_st_i = {[ṁ_gas C_p_gas (T_gas,out_hp−eco − T_gas,out_iP−evap) (1 − heat loss%)] − [blow down% (h_sat,in_iP−evap − h2i)]} / (h_iP−sh−outlet − h_iP−evap−inlet) (17) (intermediate-pressure steam generation rate) ṁ_st_L = {[ṁ_gas C_p_gas (T_gas,out_ip−eco − T_gas,out_LP−evap) (1 − heat loss%)] − [blow down% (h_sat,in_LP−evap − h2L)]} / (h_LP−sh−outlet − h_LP−evap−inlet) (18) (low-pressure steam generation rate)

paragraphs.text: Operating the HRSG at off-design conditions causes the evaporator’s performance to vary from the design point and the performance factor for each evaporator can be evaluated from the following equation (19-21) (Hicks, 2006): For high-pressure evaporator constant K1: K_1 = {ln[(T_gas,in_hp−evap(℉) − T_saturation,in_hp−evap(℉)) / (T_gas,out_hp−evap(℉) − T_saturation,in_hp−evap(℉))] / (ṁ_gas (lb/hr))^−0.4} (19) (HP evaporator performance factor from the log ratio of gas-to-saturation temperature differences at inlet and outlet, in ℉, and gas flow in lb/hr) For intermediate pressure evaporator constant K2: K_2 = {ln[(T_gas,in_ip−evap(℉) − T_saturation,in_ip−evap(℉)) / (T_gas,out_ip−evap(℉) − T_saturation,in_ip−evap(℉))] / (ṁ_gas (lb/hr))^−0.4} (20) (IP evaporator performance factor) For low-pressure evaporator constant K3: K_3 = {ln[(T_gas,in_Lp−evap(℉) − T_saturation,in_Lp−evap(℉)) / (T_gas,out_Lp−evap(℉) − T_saturation,in_Lp−evap(℉))] / (ṁ_gas (lb/hr))^−0.4} (21) (LP evaporator performance factor)

While, the entropy of superheated steam and ideal expanded steam are same as shown in equation (22). s_LP expand steam = s_HP superheat steam [ideal case] (22) (ideal expansion: entropy of the expanded steam equals that of the superheated steam) Ẇ_st = ṁ_st η_st (h_superheat steam − h_LP ideal expand steam) (23) (steam turbine power output = steam flow × isentropic efficiency × ideal enthalpy drop)

The power output can be obtained as follows from equation (25). While, the entropy of inlet and outlet water from feed water pumps are same as shown in equation (24). s_HP outlet water = s_LP inlet water [ideal case] (24) (ideal pumping: outlet water entropy equals inlet water entropy) Ẇ_pump = ṁ_st [(h_HP ideal outlet water − h_LP inlet water) / η_pump] (25) (pump power = water flow × ideal enthalpy rise / pump efficiency)

The mass .and heat balance for the steam condenser can be obtained from equation (26) while equations (27 – 33) are used to evaluate condenser operating pressure under off-design operating conditions. Q̇_condenser = ṁ_c.w C_p_CW (T_CW_out − T_CW_in) = ṁ_st (h_st_in − T_st_out) (26) (condenser heat balance: heat gained by cooling water = heat released by condensing steam, as printed) T_A = T_COOLING TOWER WATER_INLET = T_CONDENSER WATER OUTLET (27) (hot water temperature T_A) T_B = T_COOLING TOWER WATER_OUTLET = T_CONDENSER WATER INLET (28) (cold water temperature T_B) Range = T_A − T_B (29) (cooling tower range) Ideal Range = T_A − T_air wet bulb (30) (ideal range down to the air wet bulb temperature) ε_condenser = Range / Ideal Range (31) (effectiveness) T_approach = T_B − T_air wet bulb (32) (approach temperature) T_saturation = TTD + T_B (33) (condenser saturation temperature = terminal temperature difference + cooling water inlet temperature T_B)

Unlike the energy approach, the exergy analysis approach is based on the second law of thermodynamics used to quantify and locate the irreversibilities to help the design engineers concentrate their potential on components that require potential improvements [43]. For an open steady-state system, the exergy rate balance will be evaluated according to equation (34). 0 = Σ Q̇_j [1 − (T_o/T_i)] − Ẇ_cv + [ṁ (ef_in − ef_out)] − Ėx_dest (34) (steady-state exergy rate balance: heat exergy − work + flow exergy change − exergy destruction = 0) While, equation (35) shows the specific physical exergy flow of flowing gas and water. ef = (h– h_o) − [T_o (s − s_o)] = (h– ḣ_o) − {T_o {(s − ṡ_o) − [R ln (P/P_o)]}} (35) (specific physical exergy flow relative to the dead state T_o, P_o)

The combustion chamber exergy destruction occurs due to the physical properties, chemical composition of fuel and combustion gases that differ from the ambient physical properties. Figure 7 shows that gas turbine, steam turbine, and overall combined cycle net output power decreases with ambient temperature increment as ambient air temperature increment leads to relatively lower air density and air mass flow rate entering the compressor which leads to lower fuel consumption in the combustion chamber to reach the turbine inlet temperature and therefore, relatively lower gas flow rate that leads to lowering the gas turbine work ratio.

According to the aforementioned condition of ambient temperature increment, the resultant compressed air temperature is increasing and the fuel demand will decrease to keep turbine inlet temperature at a constant value which reflects on heat addition reduction required in the combustion chamber as shown in Figure 8 and leads to a lower steam generation rate and lower output power from steam and overall combined cycle.

As the ambient temperature increases, the compression process becomes less efficient due to lower air density and higher power demand to compress the air which leads to lower gas turbine efficiency. Also, ambient temperature increment effect on cooling tower effectiveness and inlet temperature of cooling water to the steam condenser which leads to relatively higher condenser operating pressure and therefore, higher back pressure on the low-pressure steam turbine, and lower produced output power and therefore, lower steam cycle efficiency and overall CCPP efficiency as illustrated in Figure 9. The power and efficiency degradation with ambient temperature increment leads to an increase in the specific fuel consumption as shown in Figure 10. For connection, the gas turbine performance with HRSG performance based on ambient temperature variation, Figure 11 summarizes the scene of ambient temperature increment as the temperature of flowing exhaust gas drops and lower flue gases flowing through the HRSG, resulting in less heat energy being available for steam generation. In addition to the ambient temperature increment degrading the thermal energy efficiency, the commonly known intercooled gas turbine retrofitting is mainly used for boosting the net output power through compression power reduction and reduce the cycle performance sensitivity to ambient temperature increment.

The exergy analysis is performed mainly to quantify and evaluate the useful work potential loss in order to refer to the most deficient component that requires potential improvement. The destroyed potential can occur in the form of heat loss, mechanical loss, or mass-flowing loss. The exergy destruction rates for gas turbine components are shown in Figure 12 to Figure 15.

The combustion chamber is considered as the major source of exergy destruction in the whole cycle. This potential loss is mainly due to several factors including but not limited to temperature gradient, inadequate air-fuel mixing process, and chemical reaction irreversibilities. Figure 12 shows that the exergy destruction rate is decreasing with ambient temperature increment. As the compressed air temperature increases, a relatively lower temperature difference between compressed air and fuel and between the flue gases and surroundings as well as reduced fuel consumption that leads to lower fuel composition variation with standard ambient air compositions. On the other hand, Figure 13 and Figure 14 show that the compressors demonstrate increasing exergy destruction rate with ambient temperature increment as the air becomes less dense and the required power by the compressor to achieve the same pressure ratio increases. This leads to lower compression process efficiency and higher heat dissipation that is lost in the form of entropy generation. Also, Figure 14 shows that waste exergy to the surroundings decreases with ambient temperature increment as a result of reducing the temperature gradient between the flue gas getting out from the HRSG’s stack and the ambient temperature of the air.

The gas turbine is split into high and low-pressure gas turbines. For the high-pressure gas turbine, the turbine inlet temperature is kept constant while the expanded gas temperature decreases, resulting in a higher difference in physical exergy by mass flow at those two state points while the power output decreases with ambient temperature increment, leading to an exergy destruction rate increment of the high-pressure gas turbine as illustrated in Figure 15. The exergy destruction rate of HRSG’s coils is evaluated under ambient temperature variation, considering the flue gas’s pressure drop across each coil is constant and the results are shown in Figure 16 to Figure 20. While Figure 21 shows the overall HRSG exergy destruction. Figure 22 and Figure 23 illustrate the exergy destruction rate of steam turbines with ambient temperature increment. In this proposed study, the steam turbines demonstrate a decreasing exergy destruction rate as a result of lower steam flow rate through the steam turbines, lower output power, and reduction in entropy generation rate.

It’s commonly known that the exergy destruction rate of feed water pumps and condensate pumps is increasing with ambient temperature increment. However, this proposal aimed to decrease that effect through different operation strategies to maximize the potential of the steam system. The feed water pumps and condensate pumps are assumed to work on a constant delivery pressure. While, the ambient temperature increment leads to steam and condensate flow rate reduction thus, will reduce the pump's required power. Note that the low-pressure injection pump operates at different pressures for maximum steam generation at the stack section and well use of flue gas heat energy for the lowest exergy destruction to the surroundings which is the reason behind low-pressure steam turbine has a significant reduction in exergy destruction rate with ambient temperature increment due to a relative increment in power output as shown in Figure 24 and Figure 25.

As commonly known, the ambient temperature increment leads to a reduction in flue gas flow rate and therefore, a reduction of steam generation rate. While the cooling water temperature outlet from the cooling tower is close to the wet bulb ambient air temperature. So, the temperature difference between cooling water at a higher ambient temperature and steam temperature decreases. These reasons result in relatively higher condenser operating pressure and exergy destruction reduction as illustrated in Figure 26.

In conclusion, this study presented and investigated the performance of the proposed state-of-the-art modification on combined cycle power plants based on intercooled gas turbine 3PR CCPP accompanied by a steam injection system for performance enhancement with extensive utilization of the available exergy of the flowing gases while minimizing the exergy destruction purpose. The proposed cycle primarily relies on low-pressure economizing water of the bottoming cycle as a coolant for the intercooler of the topping cycle for preheating. Thus, it will result in partial energy saving of the flue gases passing through the HRSG, which will be exploited in additional sections dedicated to steam generation.

The study yielded that a partial amount of low-pressure economizing water is the optimum choice for efficiency enhancement while maintaining a marginal net output power enhancement. Also, the study's key findings showed that the proposed cycle enhanced the net output power and thermal energy efficiency by 14.5 MW and 0.26% respectively with decreased impact of ambient temperature variation on the overall performance.

on the other hand, the proposed cycle showed that the combustion chamber is considered as the major source of vulnerability and the most effective component which accounts for 44.4% of the total exergy destruction of the whole cycle with a small augmentation in the combustion chamber's exergy destruction by 0.3%. While the gas turbine's exergy destruction accounts for 11.14% of the overall destruction with a reduction of exergy destruction by 11.22% and HRSG’s destruction rate decreased by 1.36% compared to the reference cycle. while the condensate pump has the lowest exergy destruction rate which accounts for 0.007% of the total exergy destruction of the whole cycle. on the other hand, exergy losses to the surrounding whether through the chimney or steam surface condenser were evaluated by 15.92% of the total exergy destruction of the proposed cycle compared to 16.13% in the conventional cycle. the exergy destructions of the additional intercooler, evaporator, and economizer were evaluated by 1.675 MW. Concluding that the proposed cycle’s exergy destruction rate decreased by 5.152 MW compared to the conventional cycle.
